en: Majjhima Nikāya 151:
The Discourse on Purity in Alms-Gathering.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable [Sāriputta] was sitting to one side...
The Blessed One said this to Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, your faculties are serene; the color of your skin is purified and radiant.
Sāriputta, with what dwelling do you currently spend most of your time?”
“I now, venerable sir, mostly dwell in the dwelling of emptiness.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It seems, Sāriputta, that you now mostly dwell in the dwelling of a Great Man.”
This, Sāriputta, is the dwelling of a Great Man, namely, emptiness.
Therefore, Sāriputta, if a bhikkhu should wish:
‘May I dwell frequently in the dwelling of emptiness,’ Sāriputta— then that bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘On the path by which I entered the village for alms, in the place where I wandered for alms,
and on the path by which I returned from the village after alms, was there, for me, in regard to forms cognizable by the eye...’?
"Is there in me lust, or passion, or hatred, or delusion, or even aversion of mind?
If, Sāriputta, when reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"By whatever path I entered the village for alms, and in whatever place I wandered for alms, and by [whatever...]"
‘While returning from the village for alms along the path, there was in me desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or even mental resentment toward forms cognizable by the eye’— then, Sāriputta,
that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, Sāriputta, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:

‘On the path by which I entered the village for alms, in the place where I wandered for alms, and on the path by which I returned from the village after alms, there was no desire in me for forms cognizable by the eye,’ [he understands: ‘My mind is well-liberated. It is in this way that a bhikkhu is one who has well-liberated his mind.
"Or lust, or hatred, or delusion, or even aversion of mind"— with that very joy and gladness,
Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:

‘On the path by which I entered the village for alms, in the place where I wandered for alms, and on the path by which I returned from the village after alms—was there, in those instances, anything among sounds cognizable by the ear...
[or] among odors cognizable by the nose...
[or] among flavors cognizable by the tongue...’?
"In tactile objects cognizable by the body...
or in mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, is there desire, or lust, or hatred, or delusion, or even aversion in the mind?
If, Sāriputta, upon reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus: [he understands: "There is no desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or aversion in my mind"].
‘On the path by which I entered the village for alms, in the place where I wandered for alms,
and on the path by which I returned from the village after alms— regarding those mental phenomena cognizable by the mind,
do I have therein desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or even aversion in my heart?’— if this is so, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu, regarding those very things...
One should strive for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states.
But if, Sāriputta, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:
"The path by which I entered the village for alms, the place where I wandered for alms, and the path by which..."
‘As I was returning from the village for alms along the path, there was no desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or even mental resistance toward those phenomena cognizable by the mind’— then, Sāriputta,
that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five strands of sensual pleasure have not yet been abandoned by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of those five strands of sensual pleasure.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five strands of sensual pleasure have been abandoned by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the five hindrances been abandoned by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five hindrances have not been abandoned by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the abandoning of the five hindrances.
But if, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows:
‘The five hindrances have indeed been abandoned by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the five aggregates of clinging been fully understood by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five aggregates subject to clinging have not been fully understood by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the full understanding of the five aggregates subject to clinging.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five aggregates subject to clinging have been fully understood by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the four foundations of mindfulness been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The four foundations of mindfulness have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the four foundations of mindfulness.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The four foundations of mindfulness have been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the four right strivings been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The four right strivings have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the four right strivings.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The four right strivings have been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the four bases for psychic power been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The four bases for spiritual power have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the four bases for spiritual power.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows:
‘The four bases for spiritual power have been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the five faculties been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five faculties have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the five faculties.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five faculties have indeed been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the five powers been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The five powers have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the five powers.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows:
‘The five powers have indeed been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have the seven factors of enlightenment been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The seven factors of awakening have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the seven factors of awakening.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The seven factors of awakening have been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Has the Noble Eightfold Path been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The Noble Eightfold Path has not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of the Noble Eightfold Path.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘The Noble Eightfold Path has been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have serenity and insight been developed by me?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘Tranquility and insight have not been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the development of tranquility and insight.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows:
‘Tranquility and insight have indeed been developed by me,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu should reflect thus:
‘Have I realized both true knowledge and liberation?
If, Sāriputta, while examining himself, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I have not yet realized both true knowledge and liberation,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should strive for the realization of true knowledge and liberation.
But if, Sāriputta, while reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:
‘I have realized both true knowledge and liberation,’ then, Sāriputta, that bhikkhu should dwell in that very joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”
"Sāriputta, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past purified their almsfood, they all did so by repeatedly reflecting in this very way.
And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will purify their almsfood, they all will do so by repeatedly reflecting in this very way."
“Sāriputta, whatever ascetics or brahmins nowadays purify their almsfood, they all do so by repeatedly reflecting in this very way.
Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall purify our almsfood by repeatedly reflecting.’”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The Venerable Sāriputta, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The ninth discourse, “The Discourse on Purification through Almsfood,” is concluded.
